results.content:
What do you do with a supplier that reports $16.3 billion in revenue and an $80.7 billion loss in the same six months?

Anthropic announced on October 26, 2026 that it filed a registration statement with the SEC for a proposed IPO of Class A stock on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. The share count and price range are not set yet. Tech Insider reported the same day, citing the filing, first half 2026 revenue of about $16.3 billion and a net loss of $80.7 billion.

Two cautions. I have not read the full filing, so those two figures rest on Tech Insider's reading of it. Tech Insider also says most of the loss traces to changes in the fair value of convertible bonds, which it calls largely noncash. That is its interpretation, not a number from the filing.

I keep landing on the same question. For years we forecast which lab would win. That game is a joke today. A public filing changes one thing: you can finally read a supplier's books the way a CFO reads any critical vendor.

Stop forecasting. Start backcasting. Decide what your AI operating system must still do in 24 months, then work back to what happens if one vendor changes its price, its terms or its direction.

This is what you can do. Let me explain. Read the risk factors and the commitments when you get to the filing. Then write one page: which of your workflows depend on a single vendor, and what is the switch plan.

When your AI vendor has public shareholders, whose interests does your contract serve first?

Three more signals worth your week:

• Simon Willison wrote on October 26, 2026 that OpenAI announced GPT 6.1 Terra at $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens, about half the price of GPT 5.6 Terra, with no benchmarks reported.

results.name: Jayson Hahn LinkedIn Post - 2026-10-13T15:51:56.544Z
results.content:
#Microsoft just announced the Maia 300, its third-generation custom AI chip. Here’s the track record so far.

The new chip is reportedly aimed at 2027, with talk of 300,000+ units. Microsoft hasn’t confirmed those volumes.

Before you get excited, here’s every #Microsoft chip announcement to date, newest first:

Maia 300 (2026 announcement, ships 2027 at the earliest). This is Clea, the third-generation chip, rebranded. Clea was originally due in 2027, then reportedly slipped to after 2028. Now it’s back in 2027 under a new name.

Braga-R (planned 2026). Reportedly pushed to 2028.

Maia 200 (launched January 2026). This was Braga, due in 2025, and it arrived a year late. Reported causes: OpenAI-requested features that destabilized the design in simulation, and up to a fifth of some design teams leaving. It does ship, as an inference-only chip inside Azure.

Training chip (early 2024). Reportedly scrapped. It was never announced publicly.

Maia 100 and Cobalt 100 (November 2023). Microsoft’s debut custom AI accelerator and Arm CPU. Cobalt shipped. Maia 100 stayed a limited, mostly internal part.

Three years in, that is one limited first-gen chip, one late second-gen chip, and a roadmap that keeps sliding right. Meanwhile Microsoft keeps writing enormous checks to Nvidia and AMD.

So why is #Microsoft pouring billions into a business that Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom and TSMC already run at scale?

The fair answer is leverage. A credible in-house chip improves Microsoft’s position when negotiating GPU prices, and Nadella has said Microsoft gets access to OpenAI’s chip work too.

The uncomfortable answer is that custom silicon is brutally hard, TSMC and HBM capacity are contested, and every slip widens the incumbents’ lead.

If you buy Azure AI capacity, don’t plan around Maia. Any savings are a 2027–2028 story at best. Negotiate on what’s available today.

If this is the kind of clarity you need from someone who has lived it for 30 years, hit follow now. Confusion costs money. This is how you stay ahead of it.

results.name: Peter Seligson LinkedIn Post - 2026-10-24T08:15:00.615Z
results.content:
Is an AI industry valuation of $10s of trillions built on sand or hard ground?

I asked Claude to estimate how much of AI model demand is real end-customer demand, excluding compute for training. The starting point: OpenAI and Anthropic's combined run-rate was reported at about $105B by late summer. After a few iterations, this is the rough split:

▪ Consumer subscriptions: ~$10–15B. Individuals paying their own money. Firm.
▪ Business seats: ~$5–10B. Budgeted per head. Firm.
▪ Enterprise API and agents: ~$45–60B. Real budgets, mostly coding agents, but ROI is unproven. KPMG finds only 7% report measurable ROI, and the top 1% of customers drive most of the revenue.
▪ Venture-funded startups: ~$20–30B. Fragile, because it depends on funding rounds continuing. The two labs alone raised $217B in the first half of 2026.
So perhaps $15–25B is high-quality demand, about half is usage-priced enterprise spend, and roughly a quarter rests on venture capital.

Two cross-checks. Run-rate is one month extrapolated, so recognised 2026 revenue is closer to $60–70B, which reconciles with Gartner's $64B forecast. And circular financing mostly inflates the infrastructure layer (chips, cloud backlogs), not the labs' own revenue.

My verdict: not sand, but not yet all hard ground. The core is real; the question is how much of the rest survives if funding tightens.

This is a rough estimate built on secondary sources and my own assumptions. I'd welcome challenges.

#AI #Investing #ArtificialIntelligence
